rules.title: Quick rules
rules.p1: Build an exhibition together while Wolfgatti, a mischievous wolf, slips in fakes. You take turns as elephant painters and peacock curators; the roles move one seat after each round.
rules.p2: Each round starts with two picture cards as themes. The curators request a total of 2–7 paintings for the exhibition. At this point, discuss the number only.
rules.p3: Painters choose cards from their hands and privately link each to a theme. Coordinate how many cards each person contributes. Describe the strength of a connection, never the picture itself.
rules.p4: Four random cards from the deck join the submissions as Wolfgatti’s fakes. Curators discuss the pictures, match the genuine ones to themes and reject exactly four cards. Painters stay silent.
rules.p5: A genuine painting earns the team one point only when its theme is correct. A fake accepted into the exhibition earns Wolfgatti one point. Rejected pictures earn neither side points.
rules.p6: The four shared helpers each offer one use. A round in which every genuine painting is correctly placed restores a spent helper when its number matches that round’s requested total.
rules.p7: The exhibition closes once Wolfgatti reaches six points, or the deck cannot supply another round. Your team wins with at least 15 points. Aim higher next time!

helpers.usage: The four helper cards belong to the whole team. Each card can be used once and is then spent for everyone, including in later rounds. If recovered, it can be used once again. Your role and the current phase determine which cards you can use. Available cards are highlighted during play.
helpers.swapThemes: Before requesting paintings, curators can replace one or both theme cards with new ones from the pile. Replacing both themes still counts as a single use.
helpers.swapHand: During selection, before marking themselves ready, one painter can exchange exactly {{count}} hand cards for new ones from the pile. If they hold fewer cards, they exchange all of them. Exchanged cards are removed from their selection, and all painters must confirm their readiness again.
helpers.plusMinus: Painters can increase or decrease the total requested number of paintings by 1, provided no painter is ready yet. This also allows {{min}} or {{max}} paintings. The change applies to the whole team.
helpers.ask: While sorting, curators can ask about a single card on the board. Each painter answers whether they submitted it. If everyone answers no, it is a forgery. The theme the painter intended remains hidden.
helpers.recovery: A round is perfect when all genuine paintings are assigned to their intended theme and all four forgeries are rejected. The spent helper card whose number matches the requested painting count for that round then becomes available again. After Count ±1, the adjusted count is used. An unused card does not gain an extra use.
helpers.example: Example: A perfect round with {{count}} requested paintings recovers the spent “{{helper}}” card. A helper card can be recovered multiple times during a game.

example.title: Example: which cards fit a theme?
example.intro: A theme is a starting point for an association, not a category with a fixed answer. Think about shapes, colours, uses and shared ideas. Your aim is to find a connection the curators can also discover.
example.themeA: Laurel wreath – could mean: victory, award ceremony, antiquity, Rome, headwear, leaves …
example.themeB: Elephant – could mean: big, heavy, grey, trunk, zoo, Africa, circus …

verdict.ok: Fits, with one step of thinking

hand.trophy: Trophy → theme A: winners get a wreath and a trophy. Very clear.
hand.nose: Nose → theme B: the trunk is the elephant's nose.
hand.truck: Truck → theme B: big and heavy, like an elephant.
hand.italy: Italy → theme A: laurel wreath → ancient Romans → Italy. Good if the museum thinks along.
hand.mousetrap: Mousetrap → theme B: “elephants are afraid of mice” – funny, but the museum might take it for a forgery.
hand.coffee: Coffee cup: no visible link to the wreath or the elephant. Better keep it in your hand.

example.museumText: The curators see the painters' cards (e.g. trophy, nose, truck, Italy) mixed with four random forgeries like the ones above: scissors, rose, light bulb, alarm clock. Most forgeries fit nothing – but the rose is dangerous: flowers and leaves could belong to the wreath. For a card like that, the helper card “Ask about a card” helps.
example.tip1: Painters: a few clear cards beat many vague ones. A card on the wrong theme scores nothing.
example.tip2: Painters: “I have a very good card for A” is allowed. “I have the trophy” is not.
example.tip3: Museum: for every card, ask yourselves: “What idea could a painter have had here?”
example.tip4: Museum: request few pictures at first (2–4) and go higher when things go well.
